title: Isaac in His Father's Footsteps
summary: During a famine the LORD tells Isaac not to go down to Egypt and renews to him the promises made to Abraham. In Gerar Isaac passes Rebekah off as his sister until King Abimelech discovers the truth. Isaac grows so rich that the Philistines envy him; after quarrels over wells he finds room at Rehoboth, God appears to him at Beersheba, and Abimelech makes a treaty with him. The chapter ends with Esau marrying two Hittite women, to his parents' grief.
story: This is the one chapter in Genesis where Isaac takes center stage. It sits between the sale of the birthright (Genesis 25) and the stolen blessing (Genesis 27), and it probably describes events from before the twins were born or while they were young, since Rebekah can still be passed off as unmarried. Its purpose is to show that the promises to Abraham really have passed to Isaac. God speaks to him twice, repeats the promises of land, descendants, and blessing to the nations, and proves them in practice. Isaac's life repeats his father's, in faith and in failure, and the final note about Esau's wives sets up the family crisis of the next chapter.
historical:
Famine was a recurring threat in Canaan, where harvests depended on rain, and Egypt, watered by the Nile's annual flood, was the natural refuge; Abraham went there in a famine (Genesis 12:10), and Jacob's family will too (Genesis 46). Isaac is told to stay, and he never leaves the land of promise. Gerar, in the western Negev, is ruled again by an Abimelech with a commander named Phicol, many decades after Abraham's treaty in Genesis 21. They may be the same men in old age, or, as many think, Abimelech may be a royal title or family name passed down, with Phicol perhaps also a recurring name. The Philistine label raises the same question discussed in the note on Genesis 21.

Isaac's farming (verse 12) fits a mixed way of life in which herders also planted crops where rain allowed. A hundredfold harvest, a phrase Jesus would later use in the parable of the sower, would be extraordinary in the Negev and is presented as the LORD's blessing.
cultural:
In the dry south, wells meant survival and legal claims to land. Filling in someone's wells was an act of hostility, a way to drive him off, and reopening them and restoring their old names (verse 18) was a way of reasserting a father's rights. Isaac's servants dig one well after another, and the names tell the story: Esek means contention, Sitnah means opposition or hostility, and Rehoboth means broad places or room. When the herdsmen stop quarreling, Isaac names the well for the space God has given. At Beersheba another well is found on the very day of the treaty, and it is named Shibah, oath.

The treaty follows the forms seen in Genesis 21: the powerful local ruler seeks a sworn agreement with a newcomer whose success makes him dangerous. A shared meal (verse 30) sealed the covenant, and an oath the next morning made it binding. Marriages mattered to the whole family, and Esau's choice of two Hittite wives, outside the family line his grandfather had insisted on (Genesis 24:3), brought his parents grief.
literary: Almost everything in this chapter echoes Abraham's life: a famine, a sojourn in Gerar, a wife passed off as a sister, a king who discovers the truth, disputes over wells, a treaty with Abimelech and Phicol, and the naming of Beersheba. Genesis presents Isaac as his father's son, reopening his father's wells, sometimes in the literal sense. There is wordplay in verse 8: the word for “caressing” is the verb to laugh or play, the root of Isaac's own name. The chapter is framed by two appearances of the LORD (verses 2-5 and 24), each promising his presence (“I will be with you” in verse 3, “I am with you” in verse 24), and it moves from scarcity to abundance and from conflict to peace. The closing two verses about Esau are a bridge, preparing for Rebekah's complaint about Hittite women in Genesis 27:46.

outline.t: Famine, and the promises renewed to Isaac
Isaac calls Rebekah his sister in Gerar
Isaac's wealth and the Philistines' envy
Disputed wells, and God's word at Beersheba
Abimelech makes a treaty with Isaac

doctrines.note: God repeats to Isaac the promises he swore to Abraham: land, numerous descendants, and blessing “through your offspring” for “all nations of the earth” (verse 4). The covenant passes from one generation to the next by God's own word, not by inheritance alone.

God's blessing brings wealth, but also envy and conflict. Isaac's response is to move on rather than fight, and God makes room for him. Even Isaac's former opponents conclude, “We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you” (verse 28).

God says Abraham “kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws” (verse 5), using the vocabulary of the later law of Moses for a man who lived before Sinai. The verse joins faith and obedience: Abraham's trust showed itself in doing what God said (see the hard question).

words.note: Tsachaq, to laugh, play, or, as in verse 8, caress. It is the root of Isaac's name (he laughs). The narrator uses it with a smile: Abimelech sees Isaac isaac-ing with Rebekah, and the tenderness gives the lie away. The same root appeared at Isaac's birth (Genesis 21:6) and in Ishmael's behavior (21:9).

Rachav, to be wide or to make room. Isaac explains the name Rehoboth with it: “At last the LORD has made room for us” (verse 22). In the Psalms the same verb describes God setting someone free from distress, putting him in a broad place (Psalm 4:1).

Torah, instruction or law. Later it names the law given through Moses and the first five books of the Bible. Here, in the plural, it appears with commandments and statutes to describe what Abraham kept, and interpreters differ on whether it means the specific instructions God gave him or something broader.

christ: God tells Isaac that the blessing will come to him “for the sake of My servant Abraham” (verse 24) and because Abraham listened to God's voice (verse 5). The blessing of one man rests on the faithfulness of another. Christians see that pattern fulfilled in Christ, through whose obedience many are made righteous (Romans 5:19) and for whose sake God blesses those joined to him; that is a thematic link rather than a New Testament use of this passage. The promise repeated here, that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring, is the promise Paul identifies with Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). Isaac's willingness to give way at the wells rather than fight, and God's making room for him, also fits the pattern Jesus blesses in the meek, who will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).

hard.q: How could Abraham keep God's “statutes” and “laws” centuries before the law was given at Sinai?
hard.a:
Verse 5 uses the full vocabulary of the law of Moses, charge, commandments, statutes, and laws, to describe Abraham, who lived long before Moses. Interpreters explain this in several ways. Many read the words broadly: Abraham obeyed everything God told him, from leaving his homeland to circumcision to the offering of Isaac, and the narrator uses the language his readers knew for obedience to God. Later Jewish tradition took it more literally; the Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, cites this verse to say that Abraham kept the whole law before it was given. Many critical scholars see the phrasing as the work of a later editor shaped by Deuteronomy.

A related question is whether the blessing was earned. In Genesis 15 God bound himself to Abraham by grace, and Paul insists that the promise came through faith long before the law (Galatians 3:17-18). Here the promise is confirmed “because Abraham listened to My voice.” Most Christian interpreters hold these together: the promise rests on God's grace, and Abraham's obedience is the fruit and evidence of his faith, as James 2:21-23 argues from Genesis 22.

questions: Isaac repeated both his father's faith and his father's failure. What have you inherited from those who went before you, for good and for ill?
Isaac moved on from contested wells until he found room. When is it wise to give way rather than fight for what is rightfully yours?
Abimelech could see that the LORD was with Isaac. What would lead others to say that about a person or a community today?
